item.title: An Anti-A.I. Campus Movement
item.description:
Good morning! Grand Theft Auto VI is out now. Are you skipping class today? Let me know.

It’s also a big day on Wall Street. Anthropic will begin trading shares after completing the largest initial public offering of all time.

That comes as an anti-A.I. movement is growing on college campuses. While polls show that a vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work, more faculty and students are sounding the alarm.

At Georgetown University, faculty leaders are changing their approach to the technology. And at Transylvania University, a handful of students started a petition to try to slow the advance of A.I. on campus. Some students refuse to use A.I. at all.

Read the full story from my colleague Dana Goldstein.

We’re also covering:

A summit in China

Three-year bachelor’s degrees

Holiday shopping

What to discuss in class today.

1. The Super Bowl of video games is out today. G.T.A. VI is set to bring in billions. It used to satirize American life, but now we’ve caught up with it. Read our review. (Yes, it’s the one that quotes bell hooks.)

2. Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a U.N. court ruled. Myanmar is the first state held accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The ruling could have broad implications.

3. President Trump met with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The first-ever summit between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia appeared largely symbolic. Read the latest news and my colleague’s analysis.

4. Iran has kept up its attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. A recent strike on a ship has raised concerns in the shipping industry.

5. A group of isolated Indigenous people in Brazil made rare contact. They asked for food, raising fears that environmental degradation had pushed them to a breaking point.

6. Business leaders and politicians spoke yesterday at the DealBook Summit. Topics included the promise and peril of A.I. as well as America’s shifting politics. Read the takeaways.

What you’re doing outside class.

I loved reading about Kate Baxley’s side hustle. Kate, 19, is a biological sciences major at Florida State University. Maybe if my college had a bowling alley, I wouldn’t need bumpers?

Your side hustle: I am a pin technician/customer service representative at F.S.U.’s bowling alley.

Hours per week: 15.

Pay: $16 an hour.

How’d you get this gig? I was complaining to a friend about not having a job, and he said he could get me one as long as I was willing to put in the effort to learn some mechanics! Almost seven months later, I have learned a lot about pin-setting machines and bowling in general.

Why do you like it? What other job allows you to heroically and performatively climb inside of heavy machinery on the day to day? Plus, I get to bowl whenever I want.

Submit your Side Hustle here.

Some universities are offering three-year bachelor’s degrees as a way to make college more affordable. (The Wall Street Journal)

A man who followed students into a dormitory and then attacked a student in her room at Northwestern University has been arrested, according to The Daily Northwestern.

Students at Cornell University grilled school administrators at a heated community forum with questions about the lawsuit from Jane Doe and the university’s handling of sexual misconduct cases. (The Cornell Daily Sun)

I loved this story in The Huntington News about Wollaston’s Market. It’s a staple on Northeastern University’s campus, and it kept me fed at all times of the day. I miss those breakfast sandwiches so much!

Voyager 1 is really far away. Like really far. The spacecraft was launched 49 years ago, and it’s now one light-day (about 16 billion miles) from Earth. How much do you know about the Voyager mission? Take our quiz.

Young adults are having a harder time coping with uncertainty, according to a new study. Researchers say increased distress about the unknown may help explain the rise in anxiety among this age group.

Do this to get ahead.

Make onigiri. These portable rice snacks are some of my favorites to buy … but maybe it’s time to start making them? I’ll try this recipe if I do.

Start your holiday shopping. Buying a thoughtful gift doesn’t mean you have to drop a bag. These are the best gifts under $100.

Stop ruminating. Repetitive negative thinking is often fruitless. Here’s how to stop.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Eli Cohen and Scott Ball were our photo editors.

item.title: School Aide Is Arrested With Loaded Pistol in His Backpack, Police Say
item.description:
As the New York City Department of Education faces criticism over its hiring procedures, a paraprofessional with a criminal record was arrested this week at a Brooklyn charter school — with a loaded pistol in his backpack — and charged with attempted murder in a separate case.

Police officers searching for the employee, Equan Earp, who was wanted in connection with an October shooting, tracked him on Monday to Clinton Hill Middle School, where he was working as a substitute paraprofessional. After returning from a lunch break, Mr. Earp was taken into custody in the school lobby, and, according to a criminal complaint, a search of his backpack uncovered a loaded 9-millimeter pistol with 10 rounds of ammunition.

The arrest, which was first reported by The New York Post, has raised new questions about the vetting of workers in the city’s public schools, a process already facing intense scrutiny after another paraprofessional, Sayed Mohassib, was charged with fatally stabbing a jogger, Katie Suarez, on the Brooklyn waterfront on Oct. 30. The city’s Department of Education was responsible for checking the backgrounds of both men.

Despite a history of erratic behavior and an abrupt dismissal from the Marine Corps, Mr. Mohassib was hired to work in the city’s schools, which would have required him to pass a background check, according to two people with knowledge of his hiring.

Parents and teachers at Mr. Mohassib’s school, Public School 200 in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, have questioned how he could have cleared such a review. Parents at Clinton Hill Middle School, part of the Prospect Schools charter network, have expressed similar outrage. Both Mr. Mohassib and Mr. Earp worked closely with students with disabilities.

“This is the second time in less than two weeks that someone cleared by the D.O.E. has been arrested for a violent crime,” Tresha Ward, the chief executive of Prospect Schools, said in a statement. “This is a pattern, and we’re demanding that the D.O.E. fully account for how this happened and that the city fix how it screens and monitors the adults it sends into schools.”

Last week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered an inquiry into Mr. Mohassib’s hiring, and the Department of Education requested an independent review of its hiring and vetting procedures. The department’s own investigators look through thousands of applicants annually, but their checks have limits: They cannot access medical records, including mental health histories, or sealed police or court records.

“At every school, including New York City public schools and charter schools, bringing a weapon to school or engaging in any conduct that compromises the safety of students and teachers is absolutely unacceptable,” said Onika Richards, an Education Department spokeswoman. “We are continuing to review and strengthen our background clearance practices.”

Mr. Earp, 23, was charged with attempted murder and reckless endangerment in connection with an Oct. 29 shooting in Brownsville, Brooklyn, where he was accused of firing a gun into a crowd of people. The police had a warrant out for his arrest.

He was also charged with weapons possession and other counts for bringing the firearm to the school on Monday. He did not have a license to carry the gun. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, according to court records.

Mr. Earp’s lawyer, Eugenie Montaigne, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Last year in Far Rockaway, Queens, Mr. Earp was charged with assault and endangering the welfare of a child for punching a 13-year-old boy in the face, according to a criminal complaint. The attack left the boy in “substantial pain,” the complaint said.

Mr. Earp pleaded guilty last December to disorderly conduct and was released on conditional discharge, according to a spokesman for the Queens district attorney.

According to an internal police report, Mr. Earp also had a number of sealed arrests that would not have appeared in a criminal-background check. It is not yet clear whether Mr. Earp disclosed his arrest history to the Education Department.

Still, Mr. Earp had been approved to work by the agency before this school year after submitting his fingerprints and passing a background review, according to a person familiar with his vetting.

Mr. Earp was employed by RCM Technologies, a staffing agency that places temporary workers in schools and is one of the largest providers of paraprofessionals in the city, according to charter school officials. RCM’s workers are vetted by the Department of Education. The company could not be reached for comment.

Officials at Prospect Schools have asked the Education Department to explain how Mr. Earp could have passed a background check. The agency has not yet provided an answer, according to the officials, who said that over the years, they have had to turn away a few temporary workers approved by the department who appeared to be under the influence.

Mr. Earp was assigned to the Clinton Hill school on Monday morning after its paraprofessional called out sick. He worked at another public school in the city last week, according to the person familiar with his vetting.
